findings.quote: Friction that stops slipping does zero work only if the surface it grips is at rest
findings.problem: The round-4 fix replaced the old zero-work rule with an 'only if' that fails the other way. Static friction can do zero work while the surface it grips moves. A coin riding a turntable that turns at a steady rate is gripped by static friction pointing to the center, at a right angle to the coin's motion, so by the lesson's own $W=Fd\cos\theta$ with $\cos 90^\circ=0$ the friction does zero work, yet the turntable moves. A box riding a level belt at a steady speed feels no friction at all (zero force), so zero work, on a moving surface. The surface at rest is enough for zero work, not required. The round-4 conveyor and truck cases are now handled by the next sentence; this 'only if' is new text.
findings.source: Checklist B01; the lesson's own W = Fd cos(theta) and its cos 90 degrees = 0 row; OpenStax University Physics Volume 1, 7.1 Work (zero work when force is perpendicular to displacement); reader rules, Added after the Sol audit

findings.quote: For an object rising after a throw, the speed drops by that much.
findings.problem: Round-4 Blocker on the speed-per-second sentence is only partly fixed. The new straight-down sentence names its direction, but this one does not say 'straight up'. For a ball thrown at an angle, only the vertical part of the velocity drops by $9.8\ \text{m/s}$ each second; the sideways part stays the same, so the speed drops by less. A ball thrown at $20\ \text{m/s}$ at $45^\circ$ has a speed of about $14.8\ \text{m/s}$ after $1\ \text{s}$, a drop of about $5.2\ \text{m/s}$, not $9.8$. The two-dimensional-motion lesson teaches such throws, so a student can apply this sentence where it fails.
findings.source: Checklist B01; OpenStax University Physics Volume 1, 4.3 Projectile Motion (horizontal velocity constant, vertical velocity changes by g each second); round-4 read, third B01; reader rules, Added after the Sol audit

findings.quote: Gravity and the floor's support cancel, so the push is the net force
findings.problem: Example #4 says the block 'rests on a smooth floor', and the solution treats the push as the only unbalanced force, which is true only because 'smooth' means no friction. The lesson never says what 'smooth' means (Example #6 says 'frictionless', Examples #5 and #7 say 'rough'), and this step gives no reason friction is left out. A Grade 5 reader who does not know the convention cannot see why friction is ignored here but counted in Example #5, and the dynamics lesson does not define the word either (it adds 'Ignore friction').
findings.source: Checklist L25; LSG Teaching completeness; content/lessons/science/physics/dynamics.md, smooth-table example adds 'Ignore friction'

findings.quote: The number $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity.
findings.problem: This paragraph runs six sentences, over the one-to-three limit. The Conservation of Energy paragraphs that begin 'Energy is never created or destroyed.' (five sentences) and 'Mechanical energy is $KE+PE$.' (five sentences) also exceed it.
